findings.explanation: high confidence. The real cohomology $H^{n-1}_{\mathrm{prim}}(X, \mathbb{R})$ corresponds under $\mathcal{P}$ and $\phi_{\mathbb{C}}$ to the $+1$-eigenspace of the conjugate-linear involution $c$ on the complex vector space $A_{c_X} \otimes \mathbb{C} / \mathrm{Jac}(S)$. Since $w_j = \frac{1}{2}(y^i f_{j_i} + y^{n-1-i} \tilde{f}_{j_i})$ is fixed by $c$, multiplying it by $\sqrt{-1}$ gives an element in the $-1$-eigenspace of $c$, because $c(\sqrt{-1} w_j) = -\sqrt{-1} c(w_j) = -\sqrt{-1} w_j$. Thus $\sqrt{-1} w_j$ is purely imaginary and does not belong to the real cohomology. Consequently, the span $\mathbb{R} [w_j] + \mathbb{R} [\sqrt{-1} w_j]$ is just the 1-dimensional complex subspace $\mathbb{C} [w_j]$, rather than a 2-dimensional real subspace of real cohomology. The correct real basis element spanning the imaginary part is $\frac{y^i f_{j_i} - y^{n-1-i}\tilde{f}_{j_i}}{2\sqrt{-1}}$. Witness: \frac{y^i f_{j_i} - y^{n-1-i} \tilde{f}_{j_i}}{2\sqrt{-1}}

findings.explanation: high confidence. To relate the cup product pairing on cohomology with the intersection pairing on homology, one must use the Poincaré duality isomorphism. For a basis {γ_i} of homology with intersection matrix P_{ij} = γ_i · γ_j, the period vector of a cohomology class ω is given by v_i = ∫_{γ_i} ω. The Poincaré dual homology cycle PD(ω) = ∑ c_i γ_i satisfies v_j = ∫_{γ_j} ω = γ_j · PD(ω) = ∑_i P_{ji} c_i, so c = P^{-T} v. Therefore, the cup product ∫_X ω ∧ η = PD(ω) · PD(η) equals c^T P c' = v^T P^{-1} v', not v^T P v'. While in the case of even n (dimension 2m+1) the intersection form Q is unimodular with Q^{-1} = -Q (which matches Q up to sign/conventions), in the case of odd n = 2m+1 (dim X = 2m) the intersection form on primitive homology has det(P) = ±e ≠ ±1 for degree e > 1. Hence P is not unimodular, and P^{-1} ≠ P. Defining U_{k,γ} using P instead of P^{-1} in [p8-2] and [p8-4] results in an incorrect formula that differs from the actual cup product / topological pairing by factors of the matrix P^{-1}. Witness: P^{-1} instead of P

findings.explanation: high confidence. In the definition of \mu in Example 2.4, the complex conjugation bars on the second factors in the numerator are missing. As written, both products in the numerator are identical (\int_{\gamma_1} \omega \cdot \int_{\gamma_2} \omega), making the numerator identically zero by commutativity of multiplication in \mathbb{C}. Consequently, \mu = 0, which is mathematically incorrect and would cause the real Hodge structure computation in Example 2.8 to fail. Witness: \mu := \frac{\int_{\gamma_1} \omega \cdot \overline{\int_{\gamma_2} \omega} - \int_{\gamma_2} \omega \cdot \overline{\int_{\gamma_1} \omega}}{24\pi\sqrt{-1}}

findings.explanation: high confidence. Let \{\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_{2g}\} be a basis of $H_{2m+1}(X, \mathbb{Z})$ with intersection matrix $Q = (Q_{ij}) = (\gamma_i \cdot \gamma_j)$, which in this case is the standard symplectic matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & \mathrm{id}_g \\ -\mathrm{id}_g & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. By Poincaré duality and de Rham theory, the wedge-and-integrate pairing $\mathcal{C}(\omega, \omega') = \int_X \omega \wedge \omega'$ on cohomology corresponds to the intersection pairing $\mathcal{B}$ on homology under the Poincaré duality map $\mathrm{PD}: H^{2m+1}(X, \mathbb{C}) \to H_{2m+1}(X, \mathbb{C})$. Let $\{\gamma^i\}$ be the dual basis of cohomology, so $\int_{\gamma_i} \gamma^j = \delta_i^j$. Then any form $\omega$ decomposes as $\omega = \sum_i \left(\int_{\gamma_i} \omega\right) \gamma^i$. Under Poincaré duality, since $\gamma_i \cdot \gamma_j = Q_{ij} = \int_X \mathrm{PD}^{-1}(\gamma_i) \wedge \mathrm{PD}^{-1}(\gamma_j)$, the dual cohomology basis satisfies $\mathrm{PD}(\gamma^j) = \sum_i (Q^{-1})_{ij} \gamma_i$, not $\gamma_j$. Consequently, the naive map $\omega \mapsto \sum_i \left(\int_{\gamma_i} \omega\right) \gamma_i$ does not preserve the pairings: applying the intersection pairing $\mathcal{B}$ to $\sum_i \left(\int_{\gamma_i} \omega\right) \gamma_i$ and $\sum_j \left(\int_{\gamma_j} \omega'\right) \gamma_j$ gives $\sum_{i,j} \left(\int_{\gamma_i} \omega\right) Q_{ij} \left(\int_{\gamma_j} \omega'\right)$, whereas by Riemann bilinear relations, the actual integral $\int_X \omega \wedge \omega'$ is equal to $\sum_{i,j} \left(\int_{\gamma_i} \omega\right) (Q^{-1})_{ij} \left(\int_{\gamma_j} \omega'\right) = -\sum_{i,j} \left(\int_{\gamma_i} \omega\right) Q_{ij} \left(\int_{\gamma_j} \omega'\right)$ (differing by $Q^{-1} = -Q$, i.e., a sign error). Furthermore, in general (e.g. for odd $n$ in Subsection 2.4 where the intersection matrix $P$ satisfies $\det P = \pm e$), $P^{-1} \neq P$, so the pairing $\mathcal{B}$ applied to these vectors fails to match $\int_X \omega \wedge \omega'$ even up to sign without inserting the inverse intersection matrix. Witness: \omega \mapsto \sum_{i, j} (Q^{-1})_{ji} \left(\int_{\gamma_i} \omega\right) \gamma_j
